newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium denies massaging debt figures for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Belgium denies massaging debt figures for EMU.

text.p: Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt denied on Thursday an allegation that the Treasury had secretly massaged Belgium's end-of-year debt position to improve its chances of qualifying for a single European currency.

"It has not been hidden. It was communicated to parliament and the press last September," Maystadt said in reaction to the allegation, made in an article written by two academics and published in Thursday's Wall Street Journal Europe.
John Laughland and Jean-Michel Paul, writing on the WSJE's opinion page, said end-of-year financial operations between the Treasury and other bodies had been "deliberately kept secret".
They wrote that they had seen an internal Treasury memo which made it clear the purpose of the operations was "to reduce the net state debt in order to fulfil the EMU criteria."
The article was headlined "Belgium cooks its EMU books".

Maystadt did not deny that the Treasury and semi-governmental organisations such as the social security fund (ONSS) and national health insurance fund (INAMI) had reached an agreement to invest the funds' surplus cash in state bonds, thereby reducing the country's overall net debt, as calculated under the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union.

He said, however, the operations conformed with Europe-wide agreed rules on national accounts and the Belgian government had announced its intention to use the funds in this way in its 1997 budget, presented to parliament on October 1 last year.

Treasury Director Gregoire Brouhns said the total amounts involved were 40 billion Belgian francs ($1.24 billion) in 1996 and 120 billion francs in 1997. Another Treasury official said only the breakdown of each of the public funds involved was to remain confidential.
"It was done last year (1996) and will be renewed and intensified this year," Maystadt said.
He said the move allowed Belgium to avoid being penalised for its de-centralised structure of government.
Under European rules on national accounts, any semi-public fund deposited in a bank account rather than in state bonds was not counted when calculating a country's net debt position, he noted.
-- Nick Antonovics, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6810, Fax +32 2 230 7710 ($1=32.19 Belgian Franc)
